title: Cascadable general-purpose photonic computer with optical memory

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a general-purpose computer that stores its computational state in the optical domain and performs successive logic operations optically. It would need to retain information, use it in later operations, and restore degraded signals so that long computations remain reliable. Cascadability means that one operation produces an optical output suitable for driving subsequent operations, repeatedly, without relying on electrical conversion to recover the logic signal. This describes a proposed architecture, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

The defining advance would be the integration of optical memory, logic and signal restoration into a programmable computational system. Optical arithmetic alone is a narrower capability. For example, the 2025 PACE accelerator performs optical matrix computation while electronic SRAM stores data and electronic circuits provide control, iterative logic and nonlinear threshold comparison. That architecture supplies an important technical starting point, but it does not demonstrate the proposed general optical machine.

significance.text: If optical storage, restoration and deeply cascaded logic could operate together reliably, internal communication along the computational path could remain optical. The PACE paper identifies potential advantages of light-based computation in bandwidth, latency and avoidance of resistive losses and associated heating along optical paths. Extending these properties to general computation would create a substantially different computing substrate. It would not, by itself, establish that the complete computer consumes less energy or runs general workloads faster.

Conditional synthesis: the direct architectural consequence would be the ability to keep state and successive computational operations optical, reducing dependence on electrical conversion within that path. If the resulting machine also demonstrated competitive accuracy, capacity, programmability and total system cost, low latency and high bandwidth could benefit a broad range of programs. Those downstream benefits depend on measured system performance; advantages in an optical component or matrix kernel cannot establish them.

Practical impact would also depend on fabrication, integration and algorithms suited to the hardware. The supplied review identifies manufacturing challenges and compatible-algorithm needs in the PACE paper. A usable programming environment would be a further development requirement for the proposed machine, but a particular optical instruction set is only one possible design choice. The supplied evidence does not substantiate the earlier blanket comparisons between photonic-device and transistor size, photon-interaction costs, or electronic RC delays, so those comparisons cannot serve as established explanations of feasibility or advantage here.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability in the demonstrated architecture is the combination of usable optical state storage with reliable, deeply cascaded optical logic. The PACE authors identify optical-domain storage as a limitation motivating optical-electronic cointegration, and their implementation uses electronic SRAM. This supports the importance of the storage problem in that accelerator context; it does not establish that every form of optical memory is absent or that optical storage is fundamentally impossible.

Engineering synthesis: a convincing general machine would need optical memory with defined capacity, retention, read/write behavior and error rates, together with logic whose outputs remain usable by subsequent stages. Signal restoration would have to prevent accumulated degradation from corrupting long computations. The architecture would also need an optical implementation of the computational decisions required by its programming model, rather than depending on the electronic threshold comparisons and iterative logic used in PACE. These are requirements inferred from the proposed capability, not demonstrated solutions.

The reconciled research identifies link loss, cascading difficulties and logic-signal restoration as concerns attributed to the July 2025 review Progress and Challenges of Optical Logic Computation. However, only a reported one-time abstract retrieval is available: a later fetch failed, and no source artifact was retained for the validated review. These concerns remain useful research directions, but their exact treatment and evidential basis in that review cannot be verified from the supplied record. Likewise, the broader claim that nonlinear photon-photon operations are costly remains unestablished here; the documented fact is that PACE implements its threshold comparison electronically.

current_state.text: Shiyue Hua and colleagues reported PACE in An integrated large-scale photonic accelerator with ultralow latency, published in Nature 640, 361–367 on 9 April 2025. The supplied research reports a 64×64 analog matrix accelerator containing more than 16,000 photonic components, with matrix multiply-accumulate operation at up to 1 GHz and latency as small as 3 ns per cycle. These are reported accelerator operating figures, not measurements of arbitrary general-purpose programs or of an optical-memory computer.

PACE combines the optical matrix-computation core with an electronic integrated circuit. Electronic SRAM provides storage; adjacent analog and digital electronics handle control and iterative logic; electronic comparators perform nonlinear threshold comparison. Its analog operation also raises accuracy challenges as circuits scale. The review notes 5,000 hybrid iterations, but repeated execution through a system containing electronics does not establish thousands of optical-only logic stages. The result demonstrates a substantial hybrid accelerator, without demonstrating optical state and deeply cascaded optical logic in a general-purpose machine.

The supplied validated review reports identity-verified, untruncated HTML and PDF text for the Nature article, covering the main article, methods and extended-data captions. Figures and supplementary files were not inspected, so the interpretation here rests on the reviewed text and supplied research rather than independent visual or supplementary-data analysis. The second source, attributed in the research to Jingcheng Li and colleagues and dated 22 July 2025, has no retained artifact. Its reported abstract therefore has a materially weaker verification basis than the Nature article; the missing capture does not establish that its reported findings are false.

Evidence boundary: the supplied material establishes a dated positive result in hybrid analog photonic acceleration. It does not establish the universal assertion that digital optical computers with memory do not exist. No bounded freshness-search entries were supplied, so whether another architecture had demonstrated the complete proposed capability by 1 November 2026 remains unresolved. The record supports neither declaring this innovation achieved nor asserting its worldwide absence at that date.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed architectural demonstration: build a stored-program or equivalent general-purpose machine whose computational state and logic remain optical through at least thousands of cascaded stages without electrical regeneration. Demonstrate optical state retention, reading, writing and signal restoration while executing programs that require state-dependent decisions and repeated use of stored information. The thousands-of-stages threshold is a proposed evaluation choice, not an established scientific standard. The demonstration should identify any electronic assistance and explain whether it participates in computational state, logic or restoration.
completion_criteria.label: Thousands-stage optical machine executing state-dependent programs without electrical regeneration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reliability and reproducibility demonstration: specify memory capacity, retention time, logic error rates, numerical precision where applicable, operating conditions and the longest demonstrated optical cascade. Test multiple programs and data patterns, including cases that stress state retention and accumulated signal degradation. Publish enough architectural detail, measurement procedures and results for independent reproduction. A finite test suite establishes demonstrated breadth and reliability within stated conditions; it cannot establish literal universality or error-free operation for every possible program.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible optical memory and cascade reliability under stressed programs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical demonstration: compare the complete machine with a strong electronic baseline on a diverse general-purpose benchmark suite at matched correctness and precision. Report workload coverage, latency, throughput and whole-system energy, including light sources, memory, control, interfaces and any required stabilization. Define in advance which performance advantage counts as success and disclose capacity, environmental and scaling limits. A fast optical arithmetic kernel alone would not establish general-workload superiority.
completion_criteria.label: Whole-system general-purpose benchmarks versus a strong electronic baseline

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scope boundary: a 64×64 analog matrix engine with electronic memory would not meet the optical-state and optical-logic requirement. Neither would an otherwise electronic computer equipped with hypothetical zero-latency optical-electrical conversion. Repeated hybrid iterations also cannot substitute for the required optical cascade. These exclusions follow from the proposed concept identity; they do not diminish the value of hybrid accelerators for their intended workloads.
completion_criteria.label: Electronic-memory engines and hybrid iterations excluded from optical cascade

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison, as conceptual synthesis: CPE-01, Application-scale fault-tolerant quantum computer, concerns useful fault-tolerant quantum computation; CPE-04 concerns general computation with optical memory and cascaded optical logic. An optical implementation does not itself establish quantum computation or quantum fault tolerance. CPE-07, Utility-scale quantum-repeater internet, concerns quantum networking over distance. Optical transmission can be relevant to both, but neither a quantum network nor photonic quantum hardware establishes the classical architectural capability proposed here.

Roster comparison, as conceptual synthesis: CPE-02, Room-temperature general-purpose adiabatic reversible computer, targets reversible computation and its energy implications. CPE-04 specifies an optical computational medium without requiring reversible logic. CPE-06, Wall-plug-superior superconducting classical computer at useful scale, specifies a different physical implementation and a whole-system energy outcome. Neither optical operation nor superconductivity alone establishes that outcome; any performance overlap would require system-level measurement.

Roster comparison, as conceptual synthesis: CPE-03, General-purpose fabric that retires data-movement dominance, overlaps with CPE-04's interest in internal communication. Keeping information optical might contribute to such a fabric, but it would not automatically show that data movement no longer dominates general workloads. Conversely, CPE-03 could be achieved by an architecture without optical memory or deeply cascaded optical logic.

Roster comparison, as conceptual synthesis: CPE-05, Mammalian-scale neuromorphic learning machine near biological energy, targets learning capability and energy at a particular scale. An optical matrix accelerator could be relevant to learning workloads, but neither that application nor neuromorphic behavior supplies CPE-04's general optical state-and-logic capability. CPE-08, Economically manufacturable atomic-density defect-tolerant digital computer, targets density, defect tolerance and manufacturability. Those requirements are distinct from the optical medium and cascading requirements here; satisfying either concept would not establish the other.

Historical comparison, conditional on the supplied description: historical item 5 is described as a hybrid chip using photonic links wherever beneficial with seamless electronic conversion. That target overlaps with CPE-04 but permits electronic computation and state, whereas CPE-04 requires optical state and logic through deep computational cascades. The original historical wording was not supplied, so this distinction cannot be independently calibrated. Historical item 5 must also be kept separate from roster entry CPE-05, which concerns neuromorphic learning. A co-packaged optical matrix accelerator alone would not establish either CPE-04 or the historical hybrid-chip target as described.

unresolved_issues: Whether any architecture had demonstrated the complete CPE-04 capability by 1 November 2026 remains unknown because no bounded freshness-search record was supplied.
The optical-logic review's identity, full contents and reported abstract passage cannot be independently verified from the supplied artifacts.
The supplied record does not resolve broad comparisons involving optical-memory compactness, photon-photon operation costs, photonic-device size or electronic RC costs.
The proposed thousands-of-stages threshold, benchmark suite, retention requirements and acceptable error rates need operational definitions before evaluation; they are not established standards.
The reported 1 GHz operation and 3 ns minimum cycle latency do not establish general-program performance; their relevance to a future general optical machine remains to be demonstrated.
The original wording of historical item 5 is missing, so its overlap and completion boundary remain conditional on the supplied description.
No specific optical memory, restoration mechanism or programmable architecture is established here as sufficient to realize the complete concept.

brief.title: A computer that stores and processes information with light
possible: People could run programs on a computer that keeps information in light, uses it to make decisions and passes results directly into later calculations. It would remember earlier results and refresh weakening signals so long computations could continue reliably.
why: Keeping information and calculations in light could reduce repeated conversion between light and electrical signals. Light could carry large amounts of information with little delay, bringing those properties to a broad range of programs.

sources.showed: They built PACE, a device that uses light to calculate with grids of numbers. An integrated electronic chip supplies memory, logic and control.
sources.quote: Here we report a large-scale integrated photonic accelerator comprising more than 16,000 photonic components.
sources.cited_for: PACE demonstrates large-scale calculation with light combined with electronic memory and logic.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate a general-purpose computer that keeps stored information and successive logic operations in light.

sources.showed: This review discusses computation using light, including signal loss, connecting successive logic operations and restoring weakened signals.
sources.cited_for: It identifies signal loss and restoration as challenges for connecting optical logic operations.
sources.not_established: A review of these challenges does not demonstrate a working general-purpose optical computer.

shown: Shiyue Hua and colleagues built PACE, which performs calculations with grids of numbers using light, with a reported minimum cycle time of 3 nanoseconds. It stores information electronically and uses electronics for decisions and repeated operations. This demonstrates a combined optical and electronic accelerator.
missing: A working machine must combine memory held in light with long chains of logic operations performed using light.
Signal restoration must keep later operations reliable as light weakens or becomes distorted.
The complete machine must run varied programs and demonstrate useful performance, accuracy and energy use.

milestones.label: Programs run through thousands of optical logic stages
milestones.explanation: A general-purpose machine would have to retain, read, write and restore information in light through thousands of successive operations without electrical restoration. This would demonstrate the central capability.

milestones.label: Optical memory and long computations work reproducibly
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce measured memory retention and reliable operation across programs that stress storage and signal quality. This would establish reliability under defined conditions.

milestones.label: The complete computer beats a strong electronic comparison
milestones.explanation: The whole machine would have to meet a predefined performance advantage across varied programs at matched correctness and precision, counting all energy costs. This would establish practical value beyond fast arithmetic.

milestones.label: Electronic memory and repeated hybrid operations remain excluded
milestones.explanation: A qualifying machine would have to keep computational memory and successive logic operations in light. Electronic memory, even with instant conversion, and repeated mixed optical-electronic operations would not meet that requirement.

uncertain: No particular optical memory, signal-restoration mechanism or programmable design has been established as sufficient for the complete machine.
The required chain length, memory retention, acceptable error rates and benchmark success criteria still need precise definitions.
Whether fast optical arithmetic can translate into faster or more energy-efficient general programs remains open.

page.title: All-optical general-purpose digital computer with optical memory
page.definition: A programmable digital computer with optically read and written working memory, optical control flow and logic whose outputs directly drive later gates. Its architecture can express any classical algorithm, subject to available memory; signal restoration prevents degradation from accumulating between gates.

goal.need: The PACE comparison below concerns a recurrent Ising solver, which searches for low-energy configurations of binary variables. PACE performs matrix arithmetic optically but sends each result through electronic comparators and SRAM. Optical working memory and restoring logic would allow the state-dependent computational path to remain optical.

figures.caption: Reported Ising-solver timings, published on 9 April 2025.
figures.note: The implementations run the same heuristic algorithm. PACE's convergence study used ten batches of 2,000 tests and reported mean convergence above 92.72% at 5 ns iteration latency. These are accelerator-workload measurements.

completion.title: A physical computer executes stored programs with optical memory, logic and control flow.
completion.criterion: A physical programmable digital machine executes stored programs with data-dependent branches and reuse of optically written working state. Its architecture is computationally universal when memory is extendable; finite demonstrations are bounded by installed memory. Instruction sequencing, memory read/write, logic and signal restoration remain optical between successive operations. Logic meets Miller's cascadability, fan-out of at least two, restoration and input/output-isolation criteria. Electronics may supply power and fixed bias but do not carry working state or recover logic. An architectural universality argument and measured autonomous program execution are required.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis; no complete-machine acceptance test was identified.
completion.basis: Searches for qualification standards and benchmarks, and checks of SPRIND's project, Akhetonics's architecture, Miller's gate criteria and optical-memory reviews, found no complete-machine acceptance test. This synthesis combines all-optical processing with general-purpose programmability without adding numerical performance targets. The 2024 CPU paper claims the capability, but its displayed logic measurements and deferred memory results do not establish measured autonomous program execution.

milestones.title: An optical memory cell retains either of two states selected by optical set and reset pulses.
milestones.criterion: A bistable optical cell retains one of two distinguishable output states after a write pulse ends; optical set/reset pulses select the state. A paper published on 7 July 2017 reports an InP flip-flop operating at 10 Gb/s with an 80 ps recovery time in a binary content-addressable memory experiment.
milestones.set_by: The all-optical set–reset flip-flop convention, described by Alexoudi, Kanellos and Pleros in Optical RAM and integrated optical memories: a survey.
milestones.threshold_quote: two stable states (“logical zero” or “logical one”)

milestones.title: An optical RAM cell permits and blocks optical read and write access while retaining unselected state.
milestones.criterion: An optical random-access memory (RAM) cell combines storage with access gating: optical commands permit or block reads and writes, and blocked access preserves stored state. The paper published on 7 July 2017 reports RAM-cell read/write operation at 5 Gb/s using 127-bit pseudorandom patterns and bit-error-ratio characterization at 10⁻⁹.
milestones.set_by: The optical RAM functional convention, distinguished from simple latching in the section From elementary optical memory cells to optical random access memories (RAMs) of Alexoudi et al.
milestones.threshold_quote: complete optical RAMs with controllable access at any random time

milestones.title: Optical logic restores signals, isolates input from output and drives at least two later gates.
milestones.criterion: A logically complete optical gate set, such as NAND or NOR, drives at least two subsequent gates with compatible wavelength, beam and pulse shape; restores signal levels and beam/pulse quality; and isolates input from output. Data are not electrically regenerated between gates. Smith reported cascadable InSb and ZnSe circuits and restoring logic at the OSA meeting held from 19 October 1986 to 25 October 1986; that abstract does not establish all these criteria together.
milestones.set_by: Miller's essential optical-logic criteria, published in Are optical transistors the logical next step? and reproduced by Akhetonics in its architecture paper.
milestones.threshold_quote: The output of one stage must be sufficient to drive the inputs of at least two subsequent stages

milestones.title: An optical datapath completes subtraction, write-back and a branch for a result of zero or less.
milestones.criterion: For the published four-operand SUBLEQ variant, read M[A] and M[B], write M[C] = M[A] − M[B], and select address J if M[C] ≤ 0, otherwise the next instruction. Data, write-back and next-address selection remain optical. This tests one instruction cycle before autonomous program execution. The CPU paper published on 10 September 2024 claims a 2-bit all-optical implementation; its author manuscript shows full-adder and three-input NAND responses before regeneration and defers custom memory results.
milestones.set_by: The universal single-instruction computer convention established by Mavaddat and Parhami, applied optically by Akhetonics. The four-operand SUBLEQ formulation is specified in Section II-A and Figure 9 of Kissner et al.
milestones.threshold_quote: subtract and branch if less-than or equal to zero

not_found: The supplied Progress and Challenges of Optical Logic Computation review, its PDF and its SciEngine mirror could not be opened.
No measured optical-only stored-program execution trace was found in the Akhetonics author manuscript.
No externally specified minimum cascade depth, working-memory capacity or whole-system error rate was found for a complete all-optical general-purpose computer.

results.finding: One microdisk optical memory cell switched between two stable states using 1.8 fJ optical pulses.
results.detail: The electrically pumped cell retained a distinguishable lasing state after the optical pulse. The text does not establish the manuscript’s publication or peer-review status.
results.quote:
Even after the pulse has passed th rough, the microdisk laser will stay in the

becomes low. Similarly, the CW dominant stat e can be recovered by in jecting an optical set 
pulse from the right side (Fig. 3(d) and 3(e)).

results.finding: Polariton logic: two cascaded NOT gates demonstrated; the second reached approximately −13 dB extinction.
results.detail: A universal NOR gate was also demonstrated, but fan-out to two later gates was projected from an assumed threshold, not demonstrated. The text does not establish signal and pulse-quality restoration and input–output isolation together.
results.quote: We observe that the extinction ratio reaches a plateau at ≈−13 dB due to the exciton-reservoir depletion at the second gate.

results.finding: Authors report a 2-bit all-optical CPU implementation; sample size not reported.
results.detail: The supplied text describes the four-operand SUBLEQ architecture but does not report a completed cycle demonstrating optical subtraction, memory write-back and next-address selection together.
results.quote: For this demonstration we implemented a URISC architecture capable of running any classical piece of software all-optically and present a comprehensive architectural framework for all-optical computing to go beyond.
